slides.title: Symptom vs Problem
rows: One rule is matching normal activity
The integration is retrying on timeout

slides.title: Three Questions That Make a Problem Statement
items: What exactly is happening? — observable, specific, no interpretation.
When did it start? — and what else changed at that time.
What is the scope? — one host, one team, one site, or everything.
And the one people forget: what is NOT affected? That boundary line eliminates half the possible causes before anyone touches a keyboard.

left.head: BAD
items: "The SIEM is broken."
Four words.
No start time. No scope. No boundary. No evidence.
Nobody can start work from this.

right.head: GOOD
items: "Since approximately 14:20 today, four Manila servers (SRV-MNL-01 to 04) have shown no events in the dashboard.
All other hosts are reporting normally.
The four affected hosts respond to ping."
Longer — and that is fine.

slides.title: The Five Whys
body: ## PROBLEM: The same detection reappears on WKS-118 every morning.
**Why?** AV detects and cleans the file each morning.
**Why does it come back?** Something writes it back to disk.
**Why?** A scheduled task runs at logon and downloads it.
**Why is the task there?** It was created by the original infection.
**Why wasn't it removed?** AV removed the FILE, not the PERSISTENCE.
## ROOT CAUSE: Remediation was incomplete.

slides.title: Two Rules for the Five Whys

left.head: STOP AT THE FIRST FIX
items: Stop when the answer is something you can act on tonight.
"Remove the scheduled task" = stop here.
"Because AV products only remove files" = one why too far. That is a complaint about product design, not tonight's fix.

right.head: IF IT'S A PERSON, BACK UP
items: "Because the user clicked a link" is true and it does not help at 2 AM.
Awareness training is a real fix — it is not yours to implement and it does not stop the redirect this afternoon.
Find the technical cause first.

slides.title: Six Places a SOC Fault Hides
rows: Is the service running? Right version? Right config?
Can the host reach the server? Is a rule blocking it?
Is the manager up? Disk full? Accepting writes?
Did somebody change a rule, filter, or log level?
Did it reboot? Is it patched? Is it even powered on?
Is there a change notice? Did somebody do this on purpose?

slides.title: The Question That Saves Your Night
body: ## "Which of these can I test in under five minutes?"
You will always have twelve possible causes.
Test the cheap ones first.
**Ask what is still WORKING.** If other hosts are still reporting, the entire Server branch disappears in sixty seconds.
Five minutes of `ping` and `Get-Service` eliminates half the fishbone.

slides.title: Choosing a Corrective Action — In This Order
items: Is it within my authority? If no, it is not an option — it is an escalation.
Is it reversible? Prefer the fix you can undo.
Is it the smallest thing that could work? Restart the service before you reboot the host.
Write down THREE options before you choose one. The first idea is often the most expensive.

slides.title: The Action Plan — Seven Fields
rows: One paragraph: what, when, scope, boundary
The root cause, stated as something changeable
Numbered steps — each one a single verifiable act
A named person or role per step
A time or deadline per step
The observable test — with a number
The fallback, and who to escalate to

left.head: NOT TESTABLE
items: "Monitoring restored"
"Seems fixed"
"The user says it's okay now"
A host that reports for two minutes and dies again would pass every one of these.

right.head: TESTABLE
items: "Events arriving from all four hosts, and still arriving 30 minutes later"
"No detection at the 08:05–08:20 window for three consecutive working days"
A number, and a time.

slides.title: One Plan, Three Audiences
rows: Technical detail, what you already tested, what you need from them — and the ASK
What is happening, whether they are affected, when they hear next
Everything, in order, with timestamps and who authorised what

slides.title: The Sentence That Makes You a Good L1
body: "Four Manila servers stopped sending events at about 14:20. Everything else is reporting fine and all four answer ping, so it is not the network. I checked the change calendar — nothing covers it.
## "I would like to restart the agent service on one of them as a test. Are you happy for me to do that?"
You did not just report a problem.
You arrived with a proposed next step and asked for authority.
**Your L2 has to say one word.**

slides.title: Never Say This to a Client
body: ## "We are having some issues with the monitoring, we are looking into it, I will get back to you."
No scope. No impact statement. No time commitment.
It sounds reassuring, and it is why clients escalate to your manager.
## Every client update needs both of these:
Whether their business is affected
When they will hear from you next

slides.title: Emotions on the Desk
columns: What it does to your work
rows: You close things without reading them
Stand up. Re-read the last three.
You skip steps and forget to record
Go back to the SOP. Follow it literally.
Say out loud that you are stuck.
It is the engine of good triage
Give yourself ten minutes on the odd alert.

slides.title: Four Signals That Innovation Is Needed
rows: Copying alert details into the ticket by hand
"You just have to know to do X first"
An undocumented step everyone learned the hard way
A rule that fires on a scheduled backup job
A real alert buried under false positives

slides.title: The Best Improvement Is Usually Boring
body: **Add one line to the handover template: "changes in effect tonight".**
It is the smallest idea on the list. It is also one of the best:
It costs nothing
An L1 can just do it
It prevents an entire category of wasted work
## If your idea requires a budget, it is somebody else's idea.
Propose the one you can do on Tuesday.

slides.title: What Your Decisions Cost
rows: An alert triaged well the first time
The same alert escalated wrongly to L2
~45 minutes of L2 time, plus yours
A client incident, a penalty, sometimes the contract
A manager's night — and their trust in your judgement

slides.title: Key Takeaways
items: A problem statement needs what, when, scope, boundary, and evidence
Five Whys: stop at the first fix. If the answer is a person, back up
Rank causes by cost to eliminate — ask what is still working
Authority → reversible → smallest thing that could work
Define success with a number, before you start
The L2 gets the ask. The client gets impact and a callback time
Fix the process before you add cost
